title: Cardiovascular Drift and Maximal Oxygen Uptake during Running and Cycling in the Heat
authors: Wingo JE, Stone T, Ng J
population: Seven active men (age 25 +/- 6 y) exercising at 60% VO2max in 35 C for 15 or 45 min of running or cycling, then a graded test
findings: Between 15 and 45 min, heart rate rose 19% (running) and 17% (cycling) and stroke volume fell 20% and 15%; modes did not differ (all P>0.05).
Decrements in VO2peak did not differ between modes (95% CI for difference in change scores -0.2 to 0.3) despite a 1.8 C larger core-to-skin gradient in running.
Authors conclude CV strain indexed as drift corresponds to reduced VO2max irrespective of mode or thermal gradient, so upward HR drift reflects increased relative metabolic intensity (%VO2max).
limitations: Seven men only; 30 min of drift window (15 to 45 min); the abstract reports no hydration manipulation and no absolute VO2max loss; running drift at temperate temperature not compared.
implications: In the heat, rising HR at fixed pace means rising relative intensity because capacity is falling; do not treat it only as measurement noise. For hot long runs steer by pace, RPE and temperature-adjusted effort rather than holding a fixed HR zone.
Tag runs with ambient temperature; do not compare drift between hot and temperate runs without a temperature adjustment (the magnitude of the adjustment is not justified by this paper).

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2020 Sep;52(9):1924-1932). Removed the researcher's unverifiable 'no hydration manipulation' claim from the findings/limitations and recorded that the abstract does not report one.
